'''''Picea sitchensis''''', the '''Sitka spruce''', is a large, [[conifer]]ous, [[evergreen]] tree growing to just over {{Convert|100|m|sp=us}} tall,<ref name="MonumentalTrees">{{cite web |title=Sitka Spruce in Redwood National Park, Redwood National Park, California, United States |url=https://www.monumentaltrees.com/en/usa/california/delnortecounty/4462_redwoodnationalpark/52922/ |website=Monumental Trees |access-date=2024-07-24}}</ref> with a trunk [[diameter at breast height]] that can exceed 5 m (16 ft). It is by far the largest species of [[spruce]] and the fifth-largest conifer in the world (behind [[Sequoiadendron giganteum|giant sequoia]], [[Sequoia sempervirens|coast redwood]], [[Agathis australis|kauri]], and [[Thuja plicata|western redcedar]]),<ref>{{cite web|url=http://conifers.org/ar/Agathis_australis.php|title=Agathis australis|publisher=Conifers|access-date=9 April 2012}}</ref> and the third-tallest tree species (after coast redwood and [[Cupressus austrotibetica|South Tibetan cypress]]). The Sitka spruce is one of only three species [[List of superlative trees|documented]] to exceed {{cvt|100|m|ft|-1}} in height.<ref name="MonumentalTrees"/>  Its name is derived from the community of [[Sitka, Alaska|Sitka]] in southeast Alaska, where it is prevalent. Its range hugs the western coast of Canada and the US and continues south into northern California.

==Description==
[[File:Picea sitchensis1.jpg|thumb|upright|Foliage, mature seed cone, and (center) old pollen cone]]
The [[Bark (botany)|bark]] is thin and scaly, flaking off in small, circular plates {{convert|5|–|20|cm|frac=2|sp=us}} across. The inner bark is reddish-brown.<ref name="Arno-2020">{{Cite book |last1=Arno |first1=Stephen F. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=qDD4DwAAQBAJ |title=Northwest Trees: Identifying & Understanding the Region's Native Trees |last2=Hammerly |first2=Ramona P. |publisher=[[Mountaineers Books]] |year=2020 |isbn=978-1-68051-329-5 |edition=field guide |location=Seattle, Washington |pages=83–91 |language=en-us |oclc=1141235469 |orig-date=1977}}</ref> The crown is broad conic in young trees, becoming cylindric in older trees; old trees may not have branches lower than {{convert|30|–|40|m|ft|sp=us}}. The shoots are very pale buff-brown, almost white, and glabrous (hairless), but with prominent [[pulvini]]. The [[leaves]] are stiff, sharp, and needle-like, 15–25 millimeters long, flattened in cross-section,<ref name="Arno-2020" /> dark glaucous blue-green above with two or three thin lines of [[stomata]], and blue-white below with two dense bands of stomata.

The [[conifer cone|cones]] are pendulous, slender cylindrical, {{convert|6|–|10|cm|abbr=on|frac=2}} long<ref>{{cite web|url=http://oregonstate.edu/dept/ldplants/pisi.htm|title=Picea sitchensis |publisher=Oregon State University|access-date=9 April 2012}}</ref> and {{convert|2|cm|in|frac=4|abbr=on}} broad when closed, opening to {{convert|3|cm|in|frac=4|abbr=on}} broad. They have thin, flexible scales {{convert|15|–|20|mm|in|frac=8|abbr=on}} long; the bracts just above the scales are the longest of any spruce, occasionally just exserted and visible on the closed cones. They are green or reddish, maturing pale brown 5–7 months after pollination. The [[seed]]s are black, {{convert|3|mm|in|frac=16|abbr=on}} long, with a slender, {{convert|7|–|9|mm|in|frac=16|abbr=on}} long pale brown wing.

===Size===
More than a century of logging has left only a remnant of the spruce forest. The largest trees were cut long before careful measurements could be made. Trees over {{convert|90|m|ft|abbr=on}} tall may still be seen in [[Pacific Rim National Park]] and [[Carmanah Walbran Provincial Park]] on [[Vancouver Island]], British Columbia (the Carmanah Giant, at {{convert|96|m|ft|abbr=on}} tall, is the tallest tree in Canada),<ref>{{Cite book |last=Stoltmann |first=Randy |title=Hiking the ancient forests of British Columbia and Washington |date=1996 |publisher=Lone Pine |isbn=1-55105-045-5 |location=Vancouver, B.C. |language=en |oclc=35161377}}</ref> and in [[Olympic National Park]], [[Washington (state)|Washington]] and [[Redwood National and State Parks|Redwood National Park]], California (United States), the latter of which houses the tallest individual measuring at 100.2 meters or 329 feet tall;<ref name="MonumentalTrees"/> two others at the last site are just over 96 m tall.<ref name=GD>{{cite web |url=http://www.conifers.org/pi/Picea_sitchensis.php |work=Gymnosperm Database|title=Picea sitchensis |access-date=2019-07-15 |quote=This tree also has a sign nearby proclaiming it to be 'the world's largest spruce'. The two tallest on record, 96.7 m and 96.4 m, are in Prairie Creek Redwoods State Park, California}}</ref> The Queets Spruce is the largest in the world with a trunk volume of {{convert|346|m3|cuft|abbr=on}}, a height of {{convert|74.6|m|ftin|abbr=on}}, and a {{convert|4.4|m|ftin|abbr=on|adj=on}} [[Diameter at breast height|dbh]].<ref>{{Cite book|title=Champion trees of washington state.|last=Van Pelt, Robert.|date=2015|publisher=Univ of Washington Press|isbn=978-0-295-99745-2|location=Seattle, Washington, USA|oclc=921868759}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-06-26 |title=The 100.2 m tall Sitka Spruce {{!}} Wondermondo |url=https://www.wondermondo.com/100-2-m-tallest-sitka-spruce/ |access-date=2023-09-30 |website=www.wondermondo.com |language=en-us}}</ref> It is located near the [[Queets River]] in [[Olympic National Park]], about {{convert|26|km|mi|abbr=on}} from the Pacific Ocean. Another specimen, from [[Necanicum River|Klootchy Creek Park]], Oregon, was previously recorded to be the largest with a circumference of {{convert|15|m|ft}} and height of {{convert|66|m|ft}}.

===Age===
Sitka spruce is a long-lived tree, with the oldest known individual just under 600 years old.<ref name=GD/> Because it grows rapidly under favorable conditions, large size may not indicate exceptional age. The Queets Spruce has been estimated to be only 350 to 450 years old, but adds more than a cubic meter of wood each year.<ref>{{cite book| title=Forest Giants of the Pacific Coast| last=Van Pelt| first=Robert| publisher=University of Washington Press| year=2001| isbn=0-295-98140-7| url-access=registration| url=https://archive.org/details/forestgiantsofpa0000vanp}}</ref>

===Root system===
Because it grows in extremely wet and poorly-drained soil, the Sitka spruce has a shallow [[Root#Architecture|root system]] with long lateral roots and few branchings. This also makes it susceptible to wind throw.<ref name=usfs>{{cite web|url=http://www.fs.fed.us/database/feis/plants/tree/picsit/all.html|title=Index of Species Information: Picea sitchensis|work=Fire Effects Information System|publisher=U.S. Forest Service|access-date=3 July 2015}}</ref>

===Burls===
In the Olympic National Forest in Washington, Sitka spruce trees near the ocean sometimes develop [[burl]]s.

According to a guidebook entitled ''Olympic Peninsula'', "Damage to the tip or the bud of a Sitka spruce causes the growth cells to divide more rapidly than normal to form this swelling or burl. Even though the burls may look menacing, they do not affect the overall tree growth."<ref>{{cite book|first=Michael T. |last=Sedam |title=The Olympic Peninsula: The Grace & Grandeur |page=109 |publisher=Voyageur Press |year=2002 |isbn=978-0-89658-458-7}}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
DNA analysis<ref name="Ran">{{cite journal |last1=Ran |first1=J. H. |last2=Wei |first2=X. X. |last3=Wang |first3=X. Q. |year=2006 |title=Molecular phylogeny and biogeography of ''Picea'' (Pinaceae): Implications for phylogeographical studies using cytoplasmic haplotypes |journal=[[Molecular Phylogenetics and Evolution|Mol Phylogenet Evol]] |volume=41 |issue=2 |pages=405–419 |doi=10.1016/j.ympev.2006.05.039 |pmid=16839785 |bibcode=2006MolPE..41..405R }}</ref><ref name="Sigurgeirsson">{{cite journal |last1=Sigurgeirsson |first1=A. |last2=Szmidt |first2=A. E. |year=1993 |title=Phylogenetic and biogeographic implications of chloroplast DNA variation in Picea |journal=Nordic Journal of Botany |volume=13 |issue=3 |pages=233–246 |doi=10.1111/j.1756-1051.1993.tb00043.x |bibcode=1993NorJB..13..233S }}</ref> has shown that only ''[[Picea breweriana|P. breweriana]]'' has a more [[Basal (phylogenetics)|basal]] position than Sitka spruce to the rest of the spruce. The other 33 species of spruce are more [[Synapomorphy|derived]], which suggests that ''Picea'' originated in North America.<ref name=Ran/>

==Distribution and habitat==
[[File:Sitka Spruce forest.jpg|thumb|upright=1.33|Sitka spruce forest in the [[Olympic Mountains]], [[Washington (state)|Washington]]]]
Sitka spruce is native to the west coast of North America, with its northwestern limit on [[Kenai Peninsula]], [[Alaska]], and its southeastern limit near [[Fort Bragg, California|Fort Bragg]] in northern California.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Griffin |first1=J. R. |title=Distribution of forest trees in California |last2=Critchfield |first2=W. B. |year=1976 |series=USDA (United States Department of Agriculture) Forest Service Research Paper |pages=23–24, 75 |language=en-us |id=PSW-82}}</ref> It is closely associated with the [[temperate rainforest]]s and is found within a few kilometers of the coast in the southern portion of its range. North of Oregon, its range extends inland along river floodplains, but seldom does its range extend more than around {{convert|80|km|mi|abbr=on}} from the Pacific Ocean and its inlets.<ref name="Arno-2020" /> It is situated at about {{Convert|2500|m|abbr=on}} above sea level in Alaska and generally below {{Convert|450|m|abbr=on}} further south.<ref name="Arno-2020" />

Forests with the species average between {{Convert|200 and 500|cm|abbr=on}} of rain annually.<ref name="Arno-2020" /> It is tolerant to salty spray common in coastal dune habitat, such as at [[Cape Disappointment State Park]] in Washington, and prefers soils high in magnesium, calcium, and phosphorus.<ref name="usfs" />

Sitka spruce has been introduced to Europe as a lumber tree, and was first planted there in the 19th century. Sitka spruce plantations have become a dominant forest type in Great Britain and Ireland, making up 25% of forest cover in the former and 52% in the latter. Sitka spruce woodland is also present in France and Denmark, and the plant was introduced to Iceland and Norway in the early 20th century.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bill |first1=Mason |last2=Perks |first2=Michael P. |date= 21 March 2011 |title=Sitka spruce (''Picea sitchensis'') forests in Atlantic Europe: changes in forest management and possible consequences for carbon sequestration |journal=Scandinavian Journal of Forest Research |volume=26 |issue=S11 |pages=72–81 |doi=10.1080/02827581.2011.564383 |bibcode=2011SJFR...26S..72M |s2cid=85059411 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://forest.jrc.ec.europa.eu/media/atlas/Picea_sitchensis.pdf |title=''Picea sitchensis'' in Europe: distribution, habitat, usage and threats |last1=Houston Durrant |first1=T. |last2=A. |first2=Mauri |last3=D. |first3=de Rigo |last4=Caudullo |first4=G. |date=2016 |website=Forest.jrc |publisher=[[European Commission]] |access-date=11 July 2020}}</ref> Observations of Sitka spruce along the Norwegian coast have shown the species to be growing 25–100% faster than the native Norway spruce there, even as far north as [[Vesterålen]], and Sitka spruces planted along the southwest coast of Norway are growing fastest among the Sitka plantations in Europe.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://forskning.no/partner-norsk-institutt-for-skog-og-landskap/vestlandsk-sitkagran-vokser-best-i-europa/539522 | title=Vestlandsk sitkagran vokser best i Europa | date=29 September 2014 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=https://kystskogbruket.no/2019/03/ligg-unna-sitkagrana-i-klimaskogen-min/ | title=Ligg unna sitkagrana i klimaskogen min | date=10 March 2019 }}</ref>

A 9-metre-tall, 100-year-old Sitka spruce growing in the middle of the permanently uninhabited sub-antarctic [[Campbell Island, New Zealand#World's most remote tree|Campbell Island]] has been recognised by the Guinness World Records as the "most remote tree in the world".<ref>{{Cite news |date=2022-09-04 |title=Is this the world's loneliest tree? The 100-year-old tale of survival on an uninhabited New Zealand island |language=en-AU |work=ABC News |url=https://www.abc.net.au/news/2022-09-05/the-worlds-loneliest-tree-advance-climate-change-research/101247300 |access-date=2023-09-30}}</ref>

== Ecology ==
[[File:Picea sitchensis Wild Pacific Trail, Ucluelet 1.jpg|thumb|Sitka spruce on [[Vancouver Island]], [[British Columbia]]]]

=== Value to wildlife ===
Sitka spruce provides critical habitat for a large variety of mammals, birds, reptiles, and amphibians. Its thick, sharp needles are poor browse for [[Ungulate|ungulates]], and only the new spring growth is eaten. However, in Alaska and British Columbia the needles of ''Picea sitchensis'' comprise up to 90% of the winter diet of [[Dendragapus|blue grouse]].<ref name="usfs" />

[[Lichen]]-forming fungi ''[[Helocarpon|Helocarpon lesdainii]]'' is found on ''Picea sitchensis'' trees in [[Harris Beach State Park]], Oregon, US.<ref>{{cite web |title=''Helocarpon lesdainii'' {{!}} Oregon Digital |url=https://oregondigital.org/catalog/oregondigital:df71wv93t |website=oregondigital.org |access-date=11 January 2023}}</ref>

It provides cover and hiding places for a large variety of mammals, and good nesting and roosting habitat for birds. [[Sitka deer]] require old-growth Sitka spruce forests for winter habitat, as the extensive foliage holds a significant percentage of fallen snow in a given area, thus allowing for better understory browsing and easier migration for terrestrial animals. Cavity nesting birds favor Sitka spruce snags, and the tree is used by [[Bald eagle|bald eagles]],<ref name="Arno-2020" /> and [[Peregrine falcon|peregrine falcons]] as nesting habitat.

=== Successional status ===
Sitka spruce is [[shade tolerant]] but not as much as its competitors,<ref name="Arno-2020" /> preferring full sun if possible. It is a [[Pioneer species|pioneer]] on landslides, sand dunes, uplifted beaches, and deglaciated terrain. However, it is a [[Climax community|climax]] species in coastal forests, where it can become dominant.<ref name="usfs" />

===Fire ecology===
Due to the prevalence of Sitka spruce in cool, wet climates, its thin bark and shallow root system are not adapted to resist [[wildfire|fire]] damage and it is thus very susceptible. Sitka spruce forests have a [[fire regime]] of severe [[Crown (botany)|crown]] or surface fires on long intervals, (150 to 350+ years) which results in total stand replacement. Sitka spruce recolonizes burned sites via wind-dispersed seed from adjacent unburned forests.<ref name="usfs" />

== Cultivation and uses ==
The root bark of Sitka spruce trees is used in [[Alaska Natives|Native Alaskan]] basket-weaving designs<ref name="uoregon">{{cite web|author=Kallenbach, Elizabeth|title=Tlingit Spruce Root Baskets|url=http://natural-history.uoregon.edu/collections/web-galleries/tlingit-spruce-root-baskets|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160918180229/http://natural-history.uoregon.edu/collections/web-galleries/tlingit-spruce-root-baskets|archive-date=18 September 2016|access-date=29 November 2013|publisher=University of Oregon, Museum of Natural and Cultural History}}</ref> and for rain hats. The pitch was used for [[Caulk|caulking]], chewing, and its medicinal properties.<ref name="usfs" /> Native Americans heated and plied the roots to make cord.<ref name="Arno-2020" /> The resin was used as glue and for waterproofing.<ref name="Arno-2020" /> Natives and pioneers split off [[Shakes (timber)|shakes]] for construction use.<ref name="Arno-2020" /> The wood is light and relatively strong.<ref name="Arno-2020" />

Sitka spruce is of major importance in [[forestry]] for timber and paper production. Outside its native range, it is particularly valued for its fast growth on poor soils and exposed sites where few other trees can prosper; in ideal conditions, young trees may grow {{convert|1.5|m|ft|0|abbr=on}} per year. It is naturalized in some parts of Ireland and Great Britain, where it was introduced in 1831 by [[David Douglas (botanist)|David Douglas]],<ref>{{cite book |last=Mitchell |first=A. |title=Trees of Britain & Northern Europe |publisher=HarperCollins |year=1978 |isbn=0-00-219213-6 |series=Collins Field Guide |location=London}}</ref> and New Zealand, though not so extensively as to be considered [[invasive species|invasive]]. Sitka spruce is also planted extensively in Denmark, Norway, and [[Iceland]].<ref>{{cite journal |last=Dammert |first=L. |year=2001 |title=Dressing the landscape: afforestation efforts on Iceland] |url=http://www.fao.org/DOCREP/004/Y2795E/y2795e09a.htm |journal=Unasylva |volume=52 |number=207}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last=Hermann |first=R. |year=1987 |title=North American Tree Species in Europe |url=http://czech.ifas.ufl.edu/lectures/Forests/hermann_american_trees_in_europe.pdf |journal=Journal of Forestry |volume=85 |issue=12 |pages=27–32 |doi=10.1093/jof/85.12.27 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060918154236/http://czech.ifas.ufl.edu/lectures/Forests/hermann_american_trees_in_europe.pdf |archive-date=18 September 2006 |access-date=11 March 2010 |quote=Efforts to remove this species have been initiated in Norway as the Sitka spruce dominates the native ecology with few native species managing to compete or thrive in its shadow.}}</ref> In Norway, Sitka spruce was introduced in the early 1900s. An estimated {{convert|50000|ha}} have been planted in Norway, mainly along the coast from [[Vest-Agder]] in the south to [[Troms]] in the north. It is more tolerant to wind and saline ocean air, and grows faster than the native [[Norway spruce]].<ref>{{cite web |last=Vadla |first=Kjell |title=Sitkagran – utbredelse, egenskaper og anvendelse |trans-title=Sitka spruce – propagation, properties and uses |url=http://www.skogoglandskap.no/publikasjon/1176375330.16 |website=[[Norwegian Forest and Landscape Institute]] |language=no |access-date=9 March 2008 |archive-date=20 July 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110720024259/http://www.skogoglandskap.no/publikasjon/1176375330.16 |url-status=dead }}</ref> However, the Sitka spruce is now considered an invasive species in Norway, and effort to eliminate it is being made.<ref>{{Cite news |title=Vil utrydde granskog på Vestlandet og i Nord-Norge |language=no |work=Aftenposten |url=https://www.aftenposten.no/norge/i/ka24X/Vil-utrydde-granskog-pa-Vestlandet-og-i-Nord-Norge |access-date=2017-09-29}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |title=Her svir de av øyene nord for Herdla |language=no |work=Askøyværingen |url=https://www.av-avis.no/nyheter/i/wwJxL/Her-svir-de-av-oyene-nord-for-Herdla |access-date=2017-09-29}}</ref>

The resonant wood<ref name="Arno-2020" /> is used widely in piano, [[harp]], violin, and guitar manufacture, as its high strength-to-weight ratio and regular, knot-free rings make it an excellent conductor of sound.{{fact|date=August 2021}} For these reasons, the wood is also an important material for [[sailboat]] [[Spar (sailing)|spar]]s, and aircraft wing spars (including flying models).{{fact|date=August 2021}} The [[Wright brothers]]' [[Wright Flyer|Flyer]] was built using Sitka spruce, as were many aircraft before [[World War II|World War II]]; during that war, aircraft such as the British [[de Havilland Mosquito|Mosquito]] used it as a substitute for strategically important aluminium.{{fact|date=August 2021}}

== Indigenous culture ==
[[File:Kiidk'yaas in 1984.jpg|thumb|upright=1.4|[[Kiidk'yaas]] in 1984]]
A unique specimen with golden foliage that used to grow on [[Haida Gwaii]], known as [[Kiidk'yaas]] or "The Golden Spruce", is sacred to the [[Haida people|Haida]] First Nations people. It was illegally felled in 1997 by [[Grant Hadwin]], although saplings grown from cuttings can now be found near its original site.<ref>{{cite book
 |last=Vaillant
 |first=John
 |title=The Golden Spruce: A True Story of Myth, Madness, and Greed

 |location=Toronto, Ontario, Canada
 |year=2006

 |oclc=62126938
 |lccn=2005001530
 |pages=272
}}</ref>

In the [[Lushootseed|Lushootseed language]], spoken in what is now [[Washington (state)|Washington state]], it is known as {{Lang|lut|c̓əlaqayac}}.<ref>{{Cite web

== Chemistry ==
The stilbene glucosides [[astringin]], [[isorhapontin]], and [[piceid]] can be found in the bark of the Sitka spruce.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Aritomi |first1=Masakazu |last2=Donnelly |first2=Dervilla M. X. |year=1976 |title=Stilbene glucosides in the bark of Picea sitchensis |journal=Phytochemistry |volume=15 |issue=12 |pages=2006–2008 |doi=10.1016/S0031-9422(00)88881-0|bibcode=1976PChem..15.2006A }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |author=Underwood |first1=Claudia D. Toscano |last2=Pearce |first2=Raymond B. |name-list-style=amp |year=1991 |title=Astringin and isorhapontin distribution in Sitka spruce trees |journal=Phytochemistry |volume=30 |issue=7 |pages=2183–2189 |doi=10.1016/0031-9422(91)83610-W|bibcode=1991PChem..30.2183T }}</ref>
